text: You've spent this course learning the parts — the ML workflow, splits and leakage, encoding and scaling, regression, trees and forests, k-NN, clustering, and PCA. The capstone puts them together on one guided project, in three lessons. In this first lesson we frame the problem, create the dataset, explore it, set aside a test set, and build the baseline every later model has to beat.

A subscription company is losing customers and wants to know which ones are likely to leave next month. That's a binary classification problem — predict churned for each customer. If about a third of customers churn, accuracy is misleading, because a model that predicts nobody churns already looks decent. We'll track ROC AUC instead, which measures how well the model ranks likely churners above loyal customers.

The plan: split first, build a baseline, compare a few models with cross-validation on training data only, and touch the test set exactly once at the end. Generating 2,000 illustrative customers with a churn tendency depending on tenure, contract type, support calls, monthly charges, and autopay: the shape comes out to 2,000 by 6, with 64 missing monthly charges, about 3 percent, and an overall churn rate of 0.344.

About one in three customers churns — a meaningful imbalance, another reason not to trust accuracy alone. Before modeling, ask two questions the business would ask. By contract, month-to-month customers churn at 0.462, one-year at 0.254, and two-year at just 0.143.

Churners average 14.7 months of tenure against 26.3 for stayers, more support calls, 1.8 against 1.4, and slightly higher monthly charges. These are the patterns a model should pick up, and they give you a sanity check on its results later.

Splitting with stratify equals y: the shapes come out to 1,600 and 400, and the churn rate is 0.344 in training and 0.345 in test — nearly identical class balance preserved. From now on, all fitting, imputing, scaling, and tuning use only the training rows. The test set stays sealed until lesson 29.

The baseline predicts stayed for everyone. It scores an accuracy of 0.655 and a ROC AUC of exactly 0.5 — chance. Any real model must clearly beat 0.5 AUC, and any claim of accuracy near 0.655 is not impressive at all.

Plotting the patterns makes them vivid — month-to-month customers churn far more than customers on longer contracts, and churners are concentrated at short tenures. To recap: you framed churn as a classification problem, chose ROC AUC over raw accuracy, explored the key patterns, split with stratification, and set a baseline of 0.5 AUC to beat. Next, in lesson 28, you'll build the preprocessing pipeline and compare three models with cross-validation.
